title: Market Sell‑Off Relents, Yet AI Doubts, Tariffs and Inflation Keep Stocks Under Pressure
body:
U.S. equity markets rebounded modestly on Thursday after a turbulent session on Wednesday that saw the Nasdaq‑100 briefly slip into bear‑market territory, but the recovery was limited as investors continued to wrestle with lingering doubts over artificial‑intelligence earnings, fresh trade‑policy concerns and stubborn inflation data.

The sell‑off on Wednesday was sparked by a cascade of disappointing earnings from high‑profile AI‑linked firms, most notably a leading chipmaker that warned its revenue growth would fall short of the sky‑high expectations set by earlier hype. The warning sent the Nasdaq‑100 down more than 4 % in a single day, briefly crossing the 20 % decline threshold that defines a bear market. By Thursday’s opening, the index had clawed back roughly two‑thirds of those losses, buoyed by a modest rally in defensive sectors such as utilities and consumer staples, but it remained down about 2.5 % on the week.

Beyond the AI earnings shock, traders are also digesting the impact of a newly announced set of tariffs on a range of imported components that are critical to the semiconductor supply chain. The tariffs, which will take effect later this month, are intended to address a perceived trade imbalance with East Asian manufacturers, but analysts fear they could raise production costs for U.S. chipmakers and, by extension, the broader tech sector that depends on those chips. “The market is pricing in a risk premium for any company whose margins could be squeezed by higher input costs,” said a senior strategist at a major investment bank. “That premium is already evident in the widening spread between AI‑related stocks and more traditional growth names.”

Compounding the tech‑centric worries, the latest consumer‑price index (CPI) report showed inflation cooling only marginally, with core prices still running above the Federal Reserve’s 2 % target. While headline inflation eased to 3.2 % year‑over‑year, the core measure—excluding food and energy—held at 4.1 %, underscoring the persistence of price pressures in services and housing. The data left the Fed’s policy path ambiguous, prompting investors to hedge against the possibility of another rate hike later in the year. Treasury yields rose modestly, pushing the yield curve back toward a steeper shape that historically signals tighter monetary conditions.

The market’s reaction also highlighted a shift in investor sentiment toward risk. Earlier in the week, a surge in AI‑related IPOs and lofty valuations had driven a wave of optimism, but the recent earnings miss and policy headwinds have reminded participants that growth expectations are still vulnerable to macroeconomic realities. Small‑cap stocks, which had outperformed larger peers during the AI rally, fell sharply as fund managers rotated back into more liquid, dividend‑paying equities. Meanwhile, the energy sector posted gains after crude oil prices edged higher on reports of reduced output from OPEC+ members, offering a modest cushion for broader market indices.

Looking ahead, analysts caution that the market’s near‑term trajectory will hinge on a confluence of factors. The upcoming earnings season will test whether AI hype can translate into sustainable revenue streams, while the Federal Reserve’s next policy meeting will provide clues on the timing of any further rate adjustments. In addition, the implementation of the new tariffs could either prompt a swift re‑pricing of tech stocks or, if manufacturers find ways to absorb the costs, limit the downside. For now, investors appear to be adopting a wait‑and‑see stance, balancing the allure of AI‑driven growth against the very real specter of higher costs and persistent inflation.
